headline: Flash Quiz: A Speaking-Focused Quiz Race for ESL
problemStatement: A multiple-choice quiz can check recall, but the explanation behind an answer often matters just as much. Flash Quiz turns each question into a class moment: students answer on phones, compare results, and can explain why an answer is correct or why a tempting option looked right.
outcomes: Review lesson knowledge through quick multiple-choice questions.
Practice explaining evidence and responding to common misconceptions aloud.
Adjust pace and challenge with modes for calm practice, teams, lives, wagers, and rapid rounds.
howItWorks: Choose a quiz mode: Classic, Calm skies, Turbulence, Team battle, Wager, Rapid fire, or Our class quiz, which draws on today's class materials.
Students answer on their phones. Mode rules can reward speed, protect beginner pacing, track three lives, calculate team averages, or ask for a wager before the question.
At reveal, Ask why can invite one student who chose the correct answer to explain it and another who chose a popular wrong answer to say why it looked plausible.
The altitude board shows the race and mode-specific standings. A boss finale can make the final question worth double.
teacherUseCases: Use Calm skies when accuracy matters more than speed, or Turbulence when your class enjoys a challenge with limited lives.
Choose Our class quiz to review today's notes, board content, or readings instead of relying only on general questions.

faq.q: Which Flash Quiz modes are available?
faq.a: The modes are Classic, Calm skies, Turbulence, Team battle, Wager, Rapid fire, and Our class quiz. Each changes the pace, scoring, or source of the questions.

faq.q: What is the Ask why speaking beat?
faq.a: After a reveal, the teacher can ask a correct student to explain why the answer works and a student with a common wrong answer to explain why it seemed convincing.

faq.q: Can I make a team quiz?
faq.a: Team battle uses teams from the Teams widget when available and otherwise falls back to two roster teams. The board compares team average scores.
Each learner starts with three lives. A wrong or missed answer costs a life, and students who are out cannot answer further questions in that round.
